Sports.title: Stand out moments from the Malaysian GP
Sports.content:
Malaysia will end its nine-year absence from the Formula 1 calendar by making a long-awaited return in 2026, replacing Bahrain due to the ongoing Middle Eastern conflict.

This news was announced last Sunday and Sepang will host its first race since 2017 on 2-4 October, though under the ‘Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia’ tag.

Despite the unusual circumstances - and event name - it is still a grand prix at the highly popular Sepang circuit, which has produced several memorable moments over the years.

So, here is a look back at five highlights from Kuala Lumpur’s time in F1 between 1999 and 2017.

1999 Malaysian Grand Prix: Ferrari 1-2 controversially reinstated

Eddie Irvine, Ferrari Photo by: Emmanuel DUNAND / AFP via Getty Images

Malaysia made its F1 debut in 1999 as the penultimate round that season, which entailed a close fight between McLaren and Ferrari for the constructors’ championship, plus Mika Hakkinen and Eddie Irvine for the drivers’ title.

This obviously dominated discussions heading into the race weekend, but so did the return of Michael Schumacher who had just recovered from a broken leg he sustained at Silverstone just three months’ prior.

Although it takes most athletes a long time to return to their best after a lengthy injury, Schumacher isn’t ‘most athletes’ and the then double world champion made the perfect return by storming to pole in a Ferrari 1-2, with McLaren 3-4 led by David Coulthard.

While Schumacher may not have wanted Irvine to be the man to end Ferrari’s title drought - its last drivers’ crown coming via Jody Scheckter in 1979 - he certainly put his pride aside in Sepang as he let the Northern Irishman by on lap four to subsequently hold up Coulthard and Hakkinen.

Schumacher acting as a ‘number two’ - ironic! - certainly worked as it enabled a relatively routine victory for Irvine, who turned his two-point deficit to Hakkinen into a four-point lead as the McLaren driver took third behind a Scuderia 1-2.

But then the post-race drama unfolded. Straight away, both Ferrari cars were disqualified due to its F399’s bargeboards allegedly being 1mm too wide and with it, Hakkinen and McLaren became champions by default.

Ferrari protested the decision though, and six days later its 1-2 was reinstated, as the FIA’s International Court of Appeal found that race officials didn’t have accurate enough equipment and that the car parts were in fact legal.

“A bad day for the sport,” is how McLaren boss Ron Dennis summed it up, but he still had reason to smile at the Suzuka finale as a Hakkinen victory gave the Finn his second title. Ferrari, however, still managed to end its 16-year constructors’ championship drought by finishing second and third.

2003 Malaysian Grand Prix: Raikkonen takes his first win

Kimi Raikkonen, McLaren Photo by: Sutton Images via Getty Images

F1 2026 will likely see teenage sensation (Andrea) Kimi Antonelli claim his maiden world title, but 2003 was the year the original ‘Kimi’ burst onto the scene. Kimi Raikkonen that is, having taken his first grand prix victory at round two in Sepang that campaign.

Raikkonen, then in his second season at McLaren, didn’t enjoy the best qualifying as a slide at the hairpin left him seventh on the grid but good fortune soon arrived. That’s because the Finn had climbed up to fourth on lap one thanks to contact between Renault’s Jarno Trulli and Ferrari’s Schumacher, before taking third from his former Sauber team-mate Nick Heidfeld at Turn 1 on the second tour.

Third soon became second when team-mate Coulthard endured an electrical problem on lap three, leaving just Fernando Alonso up ahead - the Spaniard having just become F1’s youngest pole sitter as part of Renault’s first front row lockout since France 1983.

But this is where strategy came into play, because the McLaren started with a higher fuel load than Renault. So while Alonso pitted on lap 14, Raikkonen stayed out for five extra tours and this is where the race was won, as a much lighter load for that brief stint allowed the Finn to post much quicker lap times.

So when he finally pitted, he came out ahead of Alonso and subsequently dominated his way to victory by 40 seconds over second-placed Rubens Barrichello, who’d also jumped ahead of the Renault via the pits.

2009 Malaysian Grand Prix: Half points awarded

Jenson Button, Brawn GP BGP001 Mercedes sits on the grid after the race was stopped Photo by: Andrew Ferraro / Motorsport Images

One thing to bear in mind for the Malaysian Grand Prix is its weather, which is often unpredictable and 2009 is the greatest example of that. Qualifying was dry and so was the race start, but teams were aware that rain was looming and it made the matter of gaining track position during the early stint vital.

That year’s world champion Jenson Button ultimately prevailed, having reclaimed the lead after a poor lap one where he dropped to fourth, just as Ferrari became the first team to make that slicks-to-wet gamble via Raikkonen.

But on this occasion it backfired, because with no signs of standing water, his Bridgestone tyres quickly faded away. That didn’t stop other teams from soon following suit though as lap 19 saw more drivers dive in for wets, yet the intermediates were best suited at this crossover stage.

Those who nailed the strategy were rewarded and the intermediate runners of Button, Heidfeld and Timo Glock led the way on lap 31, when rain finally reached the whole track. Come this point though, there was no stopping it and conditions became torrential with thunderstorms present.

So the Sepang race continued until the 33rd lap, at which point it was deemed too dangerous to race resulting in half points being awarded for the first time since Australia 1991. There would then be another 12 years - Belgium 2021 - until F1 faced a similar scenario.

2013 Malaysian Grand Prix: “Multi 21”

Mark Webber, Sebastian Vettel, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Sutton Images

Back in the day, Red Bull was not as much of a ‘one-driver team’ as it is today, because Mark Webber was capable of bringing the fight to Sebastian Vettel on occasion. At times, there’d even be friction between the pair from 2009 to 2013 - with Malaysia in that final year being a prime example.

So much so, it caused the now infamous “Multi 21”.

It started with Vettel being on pole, but Webber had made a terrific start from fifth and led a Red Bull 1-2 by lap 15 thanks to nailing the timing to switch onto slick tyres. Obviously the soon-to-be four-time world champion had missed out, but the Austrian outfit still instructed its cars to hold position.

“Sebastian, multi-map 2-1, multi-map 2-1, and look after your tyres please,” was race engineer Guillaume Rocquelin’s message to Vettel on lap 25.

But 18 tours later, with 13 still to play, the German defied the order by attacking Webber with an unsuccessful lunge down the inside of Turn 1. “This is silly, Seb,” was Christian Horner’s reaction, but Vettel kept going with repeated attempts.

“Yeah, that’s good teamwork,” said Webber, before being informed, “OK Mark, he was told - he was told”!

Vettel eventually got the move done and took victory by four seconds with Mercedes' Lewis Hamilton completing the podium. Webber, still visibly frustrated, took his anger to the cooldown room by saying, “Multi-21 Seb, yeah, Multi-21” while shrugging his shoulders.

“In the end Seb made his own decision today and will have protection as usual and that’s the way it goes,” Webber added in the podium interviews, with Vettel later apologising.

2016 Malaysian Grand Prix: Hamilton’s title chances blow up

Daniel Ricciardo, Red Bull, Nico Rosberg, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Rose/Getty Images

Malaysia was the turning point in the bitter title fight between Hamilton and Nico Rosberg during the 2016 campaign. The Briton arrived with an eight-point deficit, was set to turn that into a five-point advantage and end Rosberg’s run of three, straight wins, only to leave South East Asia 23 points behind with only five grands prix remaining.

The Briton had done everything right, starting with qualifying as he took pole in a Mercedes 1-2 by four tenths before enjoying a clean getaway while chaos descended behind. That ‘chaos’ concerned Rosberg, who spun to the back after being tagged by Vettel’s lunging Ferrari on the inside of Turn 1.

So, while his title rival was forced into a recovery drive, reigning champion Hamilton controlled the way out front and it seemed to be one of those days where nobody could stop him. Except, for his power unit, which dramatically failed with only 15 laps remaining causing his Mercedes to grind to a halt.

“Something, or someone, doesn’t want me to win this year,” was the reaction from a very dejected Hamilton, who’d endured several reliability woes that year. What made matters worse is that it handed a podium spot to Rosberg behind a Red Bull 1-2, the German having also overcome a contentious 10s penalty for contact with Raikkonen at Turn 2.

It nevertheless gave the title prerogative to the #6 Silver Arrows. A win at the following race in Japan, before four consecutive runner-up finishes to Hamilton gave Rosberg his maiden crown…and then retirement.

Sports.title: No more battery info on F1 TV graphics? ‘Fans don’t care about that’, F1 boss responds
Sports.content:
Do Formula 1 fans care about battery status when watching wheel-to-wheel action? Not according to Stefano Domenicali, the championship’s president and CEO.

This year, F1 introduced new machinery with power units featuring 47% electric power, meaning energy management has become preponderant in both qualifying and races.

As was the case with KERS in the late 2000s and early 2010s, battery state of charge was displayed on the TV broadcast in the entertaining season-opening Australian Grand Prix.

However, the information has been gradually phased out of the graphics amid criticism of the new regulations, as drivers refrain from pushing in high-speed corners in order to save energy, while overtaking is sometimes deemed too artificial with the new ‘yo-yo’ style of racing.

As a result, wheel-to-wheel action has become more difficult to understand, as viewers can’t quite figure out what the energy offset between drivers might be and, therefore, how overtaking moves and defences are being performed.

Asked why F1 was following this avenue given the graphics represent “important context” in wheel-to-wheel racing and there is “a very clear demand and trend for data-rich viewing experiences” in the United States, Domenicali expressed adamant disagreement.

“I think that the truth is exactly the other way around, because no one is interested in how you drive your car,” the Italian said. “The people are interested if you're overtaking or not. That's the vast majority of the people.

“I agree with you that certain people are focused on this thing that is very important. It's like when you were opening the DRS, people were not interested in what was the point to pass.” One should point out no graphics were needed to notice DRS being used.

“I had an incredible and interesting discussion with [Star Wars creator] George Lucas on Saturday,” Domenicali revealed. “He was in Hungary and he was giving me an incredible view on how the new fans are watching Formula 1. And I think that he gave us an incredible [clarity] to see how we can really simplify things, because the new fans are not understanding the truth what is behind the scenes. They are fascinated on the fact that there is a lot of action.

Stefano Domenicali, CEO, Formula One Group Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“So I think, on that, there is definitely the need for the ones that are so focused on that to have the right information. But for the vast majority of the people, trust me, they just want to see what is happening on the track. Not interested in the angle of throttle or the percentage of brake pressure on how you can overtake a driver.

“I mean, if you think, for example, an incredible overtaking of Max [Verstappen] and Lewis [Hamilton] at Turn 1 in Hungary, this is a piece of art, if I may say, that these people just want to see. And just connected to the quality of the drivers.” But how much of the move was down to Verstappen’s late braking, and how much to Hamilton saving energy at the end of the start-finish straight? We shall not know.

“At the end of the day, this is a scheme that the driver can have on how you can maximise the performance of your car, no matter if it's braking, accelerating, power that is done by the electrification or not,” Domenicali continued.

“That's what I think is happening. Of course, for a niche of our fans, this data is relevant. And of course, it is available. But as I said, for the vast majority, that's what we receive as an information.”

Above, Domenicali likened the battery’s state of charge to “angle of throttle or the percentage of brake pressure” in an attempt to make it sound less relevant to viewers. So the bottom line is, based on his answer, this data is unlikely to be used much in the foreseeable future.

Sports.title: Pictures: IndyCar’s new chassis for 2028 makes track debut at Indianapolis | IndyCar
Sports.content:
IndyCar held the first test for its new 2028 chassis at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway yesterday.

Alexander Rossi had the honour of completing the first laps in the IR-28, which is due to replaced the current DW12 after next season. It will be the series’ first all-new chassis since the 2012 season.

The new chassis, designed again by Dallara, is expected to weigh around 45 kilograms less than the current design. It also features new bodywork behind the front wheels which has been designed to reduce turbulence and allow cars to follow each other more closely.

Rossi was impressed by his first experience of the new machine, calling it “a joy to drive.”

“First of all, before you even drive it, when you sit in it, the cockpit ergonomics and design is substantially better,” he said. “It’s a car where you don’t feel as many vibrations, so you can tell the build quality is quite high.

“For pure balance and performance, it’s still hard to say, because we’re just super-early days right now. All in all, it’s been incredibly smooth, and it’s a joy to drive so far.”

Alex Palou is due to take over testing duties in the car today.

Sports.title: Featured Comment: Is F1’s use of yellow flags in qualifying a safety concern? | Brief
Sports.content:
George Russell’s pole position in Austria created controversy as the Mercedes driver passed Max Verstappen’s crashed Red Bull during his flying lap, which race control opted to cover with only a single yellow flag. That meant Russell was able to lift briefly then continue and set his lap time.

A similar situation arose in the last round at the Hungaroring: again Verstappen caused a yellow flag, this time Andrea Kimi Antonelli passed by it and set his quickest time in Q3, but he was penalised for not backing off sufficiently.

But should Formula 1 be allowing drivers to improve their qualifying times at all when they pass yellow flags? AlanD is concerned:

This is a very unsatisfactory approach. Either they say a single yellow flag is advisory and leave it to the drivers to drive whatever speed they want, (and that is a bad idea), or they stop messing about and say we’ll just go straight to double yellows in future, and if you pass through the yellow section your lap time isn’t going to count no matter what, so get off that throttle. It may sound harsh, but the point of safety regs is to protect drivers and marshals. This shouldn’t be about how fast you are allowed to go whilst claiming you were complying with the regs.

Sports.title: Where in Europe should F1 race if the final two rounds cannot go ahead? | Debates and Polls
Sports.content:
Formula 1 CEO Stefano Domenicali has said Europe will be the series’ back-up plan if it cannot hold its final rounds in 2026.

The Qatar and Abu Dhabi grands prix on November 29th and December 6th respectively are in doubt as the war between the US and Iran continues and shows signs of spreading to other neighbouring countries.

Europe has several permanent tracks which haven’t hosted F1 races in 2026 and have the necessary FIA grade one licence. But there is an obvious problem: weather conditions are generally much cooler in Europe in the winter than they are in the Middle East.

So if F1 has to find two alternative venues at short notice, which would be best?

Algarve, Portugal

Previous F1 races: 2

Last F1 race: 2021 Portuguese Grand Prix

Formula 1 is already due to return to Portugal’s undulating Algarve circuit next year, so why not get a head start? Average temperatures in December are around 17C which is much warmer than many other venues in the region.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Hockenheimring, Germany

Previous F1 races: 37

Last F1 race: 2019 German Grand Prix

The thought of Formula 1’s energy-starved 2026 cars attempting to lap the original high-speed Hockenheimring is comical. They would suit the butchered, post-2001 version better, but likely ambient temperatures in the low single digits would present a different challenge.

Imola, Italy

Previous F1 races: 32

Last F1 race: 2025 Emilia Romagna Grand Prix

Domenicali has indicated Imola is a likely venue and there are obvious reasons why: its infrastructure is bang up to date as F1 raced there last year and championship leader Andrea Kimi Antonelli hails from the area (as does the F1 boss). The temperatures will be on the cool side, however – potentially not much warmer than Hockenheim.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Jerez, Spain

Previous F1 races: 7

Last F1 race: 1997 European Grand Prix

Southern Spain offers the best chance of a reasonably warm race, with December temperatures in the 20C region. The tight, slow Jerez circuit would also help disguise the power deficit of the current cars.

Magny-Cours, France

Previous F1 races: 19

Last F1 race: 2008 French Grand Prix

Another track Formula 1 hasn’t visited in a long time which still has the necessary FIA grade to hold a grand prix. Central France would be rather chilly, though.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Motorland Aragon, Spain

Previous F1 races: None

The only FIA grade one track in Europe which F1 hasn’t raced at, which will inevitably count against it. Motorland Aragon is a rather typical modern autodrome-style circuit. Weather conditions in December would be a good chunk cooler than Jerez if F1 sprang a surprise by choosing this circuit as a venue for a third race in Spain this year.

Mugello, Italy

Previous F1 races: 1

Last F1 race: 2020 Tuscan Grand Prix

Mugello joined the F1 calendar as a one-off during the Covid-hit 2020 season and produced one of the year’s most memorable races, not least because a series of shunts meant several restarts were required. It would be very cool in December, though all those long, fast corners should help keep heat in the tyres.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Nurburgring, Germany

Previous F1 races: 19 (new circuit), 41 (total)

Last F1 race: 2020 Eifel Grand Prix

Another track F1 last visited during the pandemic, and one with an abundance of heritage. But like many other venues on this list, cold conditions would be a factor.

Paul Ricard, France

Previous F1 races: 18

Last F1 race: 2022 French Grand Prix

Paul Ricard was not F1’s most inspiring circuit to begin with: then it was shortened, then revived as a test track. F1 later returned to the longer track, albeit with a slow chicane before one of its best corners.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

I say

When F1’s calendar was disrupted six years ago by Covid-19, it was deeply unfortunate, but at least it was understood that the cause was mere misfortune. Advert | Become a Supporter & go ad-free It is deeply saddening to see a similar situation now playing out due to those who have decided to inflict pain, suffering and death on others. Compared to that, the rescheduling of a couple of motor races matters not one iota. However the fact remains that the outside world does affect life in F1’s ‘bubble’ and will continue to. I cannot think of many circuits you could drop Losail and Yas Marina for which would not constitute an improvement. Of course what I’d most like to see is F1 take in the most spectacular and demanding tracks available – Imola is a decent choice, but Mugello would be even better. Then reality kicks in. When F1 went to Mugello six years ago the cars were monstrously fast, not the feeble new generation which coast into the quick corners to save their batteries. Around a super-quick track like Mugello they would be badly starved of energy. Given that, arguably one of the slower tracks would suit the current cars better. But I’m not going to pretend I actually want to see F1 hunting out the tightest, slowest circuits so its drivers have plenty of opportunities to charge their batteries. I’ve more than had my fill of ‘clipping’ and ‘yo-yo racing’. Forget replacing Losail and Yas Marina, I’d rather the season ended two weeks early.

Sports.title: Former F1 boss Boullier becomes promoter of World Rally Championship | Brief
Sports.content:
Former Formula 1 team principal Eric Boullier will has a new role as the promoter of the World Rally Championship. He will also be responsible for running the European Rally Championship in a new deal announced by the FIA.

“I take on this challenge with enthusiasm and determination, but also with humility and a strong sense of responsibility, to make these exceptional championships even more compelling,” said Boullier. “Alongside the FIA and our partners, we want to make every round a spectacular event, designed to thrill fans around the world.”

Sports.title: On This Day: Lauda survives fiery, near-fatal crash at Nurburgring | Brief
Sports.content:
On this day in 1976 Niki Lauda was fortunate to survive a shocking crash during the German Grand Prix at the Nurburgring. His Ferrari exploded into flames after striking a barrier.

Lauda survived thanks to the efforts of rivals Arturo Merzario, Guy Edwards, Brett Lunger and Harald Ertl, who stopped their cars and helped to pull the world champion from the burning wreckage.

Nonetheless Lauda sustained serious burns and lung injuries. He was leading the world championship at the time of his crash and made an early return in a bid to stop McLaren’s James Hunt beating him to the title. But confronted with dire conditions at the season finale in Fuji, Lauda opted not to race, and Hunt won the title. The story of the season was dramatised in Ron Howard’s 2013 film Rush.

Sports.title: Featured Comment: Expect changes to IndyCar’s dramatic new 2028 car design | Brief
Sports.content:
IndyCar has produced some attractive designs for its new car but expect to see some significant changes when the real thing hits the track in 2028, says Greasemonkey:

The first change to a real race car will be the wings.

Swept wings in renders have often been a thing, but are usually worse than straight wings, and often turn straight in production. Generic swept wings have to do with compressible air flow and/or structural twist. Not a thing at Indy speeds. So sweep makes no sense at least until ground through many many many iterations of CFD and tunnel runs, which might mutate some sweep in for other reasons.

And even then, more often than not, they’ll be more straight than not.

Sports.title: Fans who attended 2023 Las Vegas Grand Prix offered partial refund | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 fans who attended the first day of track action at the inaugural Las Vegas Grand Prix have been offered partial refunds.

The first practice session at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit was halted after 10 minutes when a loose drain cover caused serious damage to Carlos Sainz Jnr’s Ferrari.

The session did not resume and the second practice session was postponed by two hours in order for track workers to make repairs. The late start meant the session took place after the security personnel’s shifts ended, which meant the spectators who remained had to be evicted from the grandstands.

A group of disappointed fans therefore brought a lawsuit against Formula 1 commercial rights holder Liberty Media, which promotes the Las Vegas race. Liberty Media has offered a settlement of $3,047,986 (£2.26m) to be shared between them, which the offer notes is “not an admission of wrongdoing”.

In its statement on the case, Jack Diep, et. al. v. Liberty Media Corporation, et. al., the United States District Court for the District of Nevada confirmed: “A settlement has been reached in a class action lawsuit between defendants Liberty Media Corporation and Las Vegas Grand Prix, Inc and persons or entities who alleged that they, and the settlement class, are entitled to partial refunds of the ticket price for the 2023 Las Vegas Grand Prix because [the] defendants had to delay the FP2 free practice session and subsequently revoked the settlement class’s admission without cause before the FP2 free practice session began.”

“The proposed settlement is not an admission of wrongdoing by [the] defendants,” it added. “[The] defendants deny all allegations of wrongdoing and disclaim all liability regarding all claims in the lawsuit.”

Key F1 figures rejected criticism of the disruption at the time. Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff angrily claimed it was “completely ridiculous” to claim the incident reflected badly on F1.

“You’re speaking about a fucking drain cover that’s been undone, that has happened before,” Wolff told a journalist during an official FIA press conference. “That’s nothing – it’s FP1. Give credit to the people that have set up this grand prix, that have made this sport much bigger than it ever was.” The FIA later formally warned Wolff over his choice of language.

Sports.title: Why Mercedes believe Antonelli was especially unlucky with his grid penalty | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Mercedes believe Andrea Kimi Antonelli was unfortunate to receive a grid penalty for his yellow flag infringement in qualifying last weekend.

The world champion received a three-place grid drop for failing to slow sufficiently for yellow flags. The stewards pointed out Antonelli’s time through the relevant mini-sector rose by just 0.03 seconds compared to “his best time for that mini-sector.”

However Mercedes’ deputy technical director Simone Resta said Antonelli had lost time in that mini-sector compared to other laps.

“The benchmark lap being used for comparison wasn’t actually an ideal lap,” said Resta in a video released by the team. “In that particular sector, the reference wasn’t representative of Kimi’s true pace.

“That made the situation more difficult because even after lifting, he was effectively being compared against a slower-than-optimal sector.”

The stewards accepted Antonelli had lifted the throttle 16 metres earlier and reduced his speed by 14kph in response to the single yellow flag. They ruled this was “insufficient”.

A similar situation occured earlier in the season in Austria where both Mercedes drivers passed single yellow flags on their final qualifying laps. Antonelli slowed down significantly and abandoned his lap, while George Russell lifted the throttle then resumed his lap and took pole position.

Resta said Antonelli had tried to back off but keep going in Hungary. “Kimi pointed out afterwards that if you compared the sector to FP3, when the car was heavier on fuel and therefore naturally slower, he was still quicker despite lifting,” he said.

“In some ways it was a perfect storm. He did react, but because of the reference lap being used, the reduction wasn’t enough to satisfy the requirement.”

Sports.title: Thomas Hearns Destroys Pipino Cuevas To Win First World Title
Sports.content:
Hearns (28-0, 26 KOs) held the USBA welterweight title under the guidance of Emanuel Steward at Kronk Gym. Cuevas (27-6, 24 KOs) received the larger purse at a reported $1.5 million compared to $500,000 for the challenger, but roughly 12,000 fans inside Joe Louis Arena backed the hometown favorite.

Hearns refused to let Cuevas establish his trademark pressure from the opening bell. His snapping jab repeatedly found the target while straight right hands pierced the champion’s defense. Cuevas struggled to work his way inside as Hearns controlled the range with speed, timing and accuracy. A sharp left hook briefly staggered the Mexican champion before another series of right hands left him badly shaken at the bell.

A crushing right hand ended matters in the second round, sending Cuevas face first onto the canvas for the first knockdown of his professional career. He beat the count, but his legs betrayed him. Trainer Lupe Sanchez climbed into the ring before the action resumed, prompting referee Stanley Christodoulou to stop the fight at 2:39 of the second round.

The knockout launched Hearns toward superstardom. He defended the WBA championship, met Sugar Ray Leonard in one of boxing’s biggest fights the following year, and eventually captured world titles in six weight divisions. Many historians regard the destruction of Cuevas as the night Thomas Hearns established himself among boxing’s elite.

Sports.title: Adrien Broner: Tank Would Knock William Zepeda Out Cold
Sports.content:
“Now, he’s a champ. Tank would knock him out cold. I’m talking about an ugly one,” Broner said on social media.

Whether fans ever see that fight is another question.

Davis has not fought since 2025, and nothing suggests Zepeda sits at the top of his list when he returns to the ring. One of boxing’s biggest attractions still has several major opportunities available.

A meeting with Shakur Stevenson carries championship implications and years of history. Ryan Garcia and Devin Haney remain among boxing’s biggest commercial draws, while Conor Benn’s popularity in the United Kingdom offers another sizable event.

Zepeda also has unfinished business at lightweight. Interim WBC champion Jadier Herrera was bypassed when the sanctioning body ordered Zepeda and Roach to fight for the vacant title. Herrera now has a strong case for the next shot at the belt.

Stylistically, Zepeda presents a difficult matchup. His nonstop punch volume, body attack and conditioning would force Davis to fight at a pace unlike many of his recent opponents. Davis also went the distance with both Roach and Isaac Cruz, making Broner’s prediction of a knockout far from certain.

Broner’s opinion reflects one view of a matchup many fans would like to see. Whether Davis ever decides to pursue Zepeda remains a separate question.

Sports.title: William Zepeda Says Lamont Roach Expected The Wrong Fighter
Sports.content:
After winning the vacant WBC lightweight title with a unanimous decision Saturday night at The Theater at Virgin Hotels in Las Vegas, Zepeda explained that he spent the year following his loss to Shakur Stevenson reshaping parts of his style. The adjustments paid off against Roach, who struggled to establish the counterpunching rhythm that had carried him through previous title fights.

“I think he expected me to come straight forward the whole fight,” Zepeda said. “Instead I boxed smarter, managed my pace, went in and out. I showed I can do more than just throw punches.”

The Mexican southpaw still applied the relentless pressure that has defined his career, but he varied his attack with sharper footwork and better distance control. Rather than giving Roach the same looks throughout the fight, Zepeda repeatedly stepped in to work the body before moving back outside, limiting Roach’s opportunities to land his right hand cleanly.

Sports.title: Lamont ‘The Reaper’ Roach Loses To William ‘Camarón’ Zepeda
Sports.content:
Lamont “The Reaper” Roach Jr. (25-2-3, 10 KOs) of Washington, D.C., dropped a unanimous decision to former interim WBC lightweight champion William “Camarón” Zepeda (34-1, 27 KOs) of San Mateo Atenco, Mexico, in a bout for the vacant WBC lightweight championship.

Roach started well, using his timing and right hand to edge the opening round against the southpaw. Zepeda responded in the second, controlling most of the round before Roach landed a hard right hand late that briefly knocked him off balance.

Zepeda gradually took command from the third through the fifth rounds, outworking Roach with steady pressure and backing him up with combinations. He finished the fifth strongly and continued dictating the action in the sixth, although Roach closed the round with a better final minute.

The seventh through ninth rounds belonged to Zepeda as he maintained a relentless pace. Roach enjoyed one of his better rounds in the tenth despite suffering a bloody nose, then finished the eleventh with renewed urgency knowing he needed something dramatic to change the fight.

Roach boxed aggressively in the twelfth, but it wasn’t enough to erase the deficit. The judges scored the bout 117-111, 117-111, and 118-110 for Zepeda.

Referee: Harvey Dock

Co-Main Event

IBF lightweight champion Raymond “Danger” Muratalla (25-0, 17 KOs) of Fontana, California, retained his title with a unanimous decision over former Olympic gold medalist and former WBC super featherweight champion Robson “Nino O Brabo” Conceição (21-4-1, 10 KOs).

Muratalla controlled the opening two rounds before repeatedly catching Conceição with right hands in the third. He continued investing in body shots through the middle rounds, while Conceição enjoyed his best success in the sixth with a left uppercut that earned him one of his few clear rounds.

Muratalla regained control from the seventh through the tenth, consistently beating Conceição to the punch and limiting his offense. The final two rounds were competitive, but Muratalla did enough to preserve his comfortable lead.

The judges scored the fight 118-110, 119-109, and 119-109.

Referee: Thomas Taylor

Raul Curiel Majority Decisions Quinton Randall

2016 Olympian and NABF welterweight champion Raul “Cugar” Curiel (18-0-1, 14 KOs) won a majority decision over former WBC USA Silver champion Quinton “Sugar Man” Randall (17-4-1, 4 KOs) over 10 rounds.

Curiel started slowly but did enough to edge the opening round. Randall used his reach effectively in the second and third rounds, keeping Curiel on the outside while scoring with counters.

Curiel regained control in the fourth and fifth rounds before finishing the sixth with a sharp three-punch combination. He continued pressing the action in the seventh and enjoyed his strongest round in the eighth, hurting Randall with a right hand to the chin during the closing seconds.

A right to the body had Randall backing up in the ninth, and Curiel closed the fight with another solid round to secure the decision.

Scores: 95-95, 97-93 and 100-90.

Referee: Tony Weeks.

Charles Conwell Stops Paul Kroll

Charles “Bad News” Conwell (22-1, 17 KOs) stopped Paul “The Punisher” Kroll (12-1-2, 8 KOs) at 2:38 of the ninth round.

Conwell controlled the opening two rounds, backing Kroll to the ropes with steady pressure. Kroll enjoyed a good third round until Conwell landed a left hand that sent him into the ropes for a knockdown. Kroll also suffered a cut during the fight.

Conwell continued dictating the pace through the middle rounds, although Kroll rallied with competitive efforts in the sixth, seventh and eighth. Referee Robert Hoyle warned Kroll for holding in the seventh.

Early in the ninth, Conwell landed a crushing left to the liver that badly hurt Kroll. As Kroll stopped returning punches, Hoyle stepped in to wave off the bout.

Both fighters were returning after layoffs of more than a year.

Fabian Guzman Decisions Aaron Coley

Middleweight Fabian Guzman (11-0, 8 KOs) earned an eight-round unanimous decision over southpaw Aaron Coley (17-6-2, 7 KOs).

Coley found success countering early, but Guzman consistently outworked him and landed the cleaner punches. Guzman increased his output during the seventh, forcing Coley onto the defensive.

Knowing he needed something dramatic, Coley pressed forward in the final round, but Guzman boxed well enough to close out the victory.

Scores: 78-74 twice and 79-73.

Referee: Robert Hoyle.

Joel Iriarte Stops Jorge Lagunas

Joel Iriarte (11-0, 10 KOs) stopped Jorge “Piolas” Lagunas (19-10, 16 KOs) at 2:48 of the eighth and final round.

Iriarte controlled the bout from the outset with steady body work and physical strength. By the sixth and seventh rounds he repeatedly forced Lagunas to the ropes, where he unloaded combinations.

The eighth followed the same pattern before referee Tony Weeks halted the contest as Lagunas absorbed unanswered punishment.

Gael Cabrera Outpoints Francisco Portillo

Gael “El Terrorista” Cabrera (12-0, 7 KOs) won an eight-round unanimous decision over Francisco “Rayito” Portillo (20-15-2, 11 KOs).

Cabrera controlled the opening three rounds with accurate punching and sharp counters. Portillo pressed the action through the middle rounds, but Cabrera consistently answered with cleaner shots.

Cabrera closed the fight strongly to remain unbeaten.

Scores: 79-73 twice and 80-72.

Referee: Harvey Dock.

Dalis Kaleiopu Scores First-Round Knockout

Dalis Kaleiopu (9-0, 7 KOs) stopped Yeyery “La Buija” Castillo (14-3, 11 KOs) at 2:37 of the opening round.

Kaleiopu hurt Castillo with a right hand midway through the round before another right sent him crashing to the canvas. Castillo was unable to beat referee Robert Hoyle’s count.

Juan Carlos Becerril Upsets Dylan Capetillo

Juan Carlos Becerril (3-0, 2 KOs) stopped Dylan “La Amenaza” Capetillo (2-1, 1 KO) at 2:59 of the third round in a major upset.

Capetillo enjoyed success through the opening two rounds and appeared in control before Becerril turned the fight around in the third. A perfectly timed left hook landed flush on the chin, dropping Capetillo heavily.

Referee Thomas Taylor completed the count, giving Becerril the biggest victory of his young career.

Ring Announcer: Mark Fratto.

Sports.title: William Zepeda Overwhelms Lamont Roach Jr. To Capture WBC Lightweight Title
Sports.content:
Coming off back-to-back majority draws against Gervonta Davis and Isaac Cruz, Roach (25-2-3, 10 KOs) hoped to become a two-division world champion. Instead, he spent much of the evening trying to slow one of boxing’s busiest offensive fighters.

Zepeda (34-1, 27 KOs) established the pace almost immediately, cutting off the ring with intelligent footwork and forcing Roach backward behind a nonstop attack. The Mexican southpaw mixed head and body shots while maintaining the high punch output that has become his trademark, rarely allowing Roach enough time to set his feet for counters.

“Shakur gave me a great test. I think he gave me a great exam. During the year I was out of the ring, we worked on what we were missing,” said Zepeda to DAZN after the fight. “We implemented some new things tonight, but we still have to keep growing to stay among the elite.”

Single counters produced Roach’s best moments, but the openings disappeared quickly. Zepeda stepped back inside after nearly every exchange, keeping the pressure on before Roach could put together extended combinations.

Clean counters continued to land in spots, yet Zepeda answered by pushing the action and backing Roach toward the ropes. There were no knockdowns, though the pattern changed little over the second half of the fight as Roach searched for openings while moving backward.

“We thought he was a one-trick pony. He actually used his feet. He was stepping back and not allowing me to get my counters off,” said Roach on what went wrong against Zepeda. “He did it the whole fight. I had to switch a couple things up, but I just didn’t succeed.”

Repeated body shots gradually slowed Roach’s movement, allowing Zepeda to remain in punching range for much of the fight.

Sports.title: Raymond Muratalla Eyes 140 After Dominant Win Over Robson Conceição
Sports.content:
Despite the lopsided scorecards, Muratalla did not believe he performed at his highest level.

“I felt good. I don’t think I gave my best performance. I think making 135 is a little hard for me. I’m going to feel a lot better at 140,” Muratalla said after the fight. “Yes, this will be my last fight at 135. It’s tough making this weight and I’m looking forward to moving up.”

The comments immediately raise questions about how much longer Muratalla plans to remain at lightweight. He captured the vacant IBF title earlier this year and successfully defended it against Conceição, but his postfight remarks indicate the strain of making weight is becoming a significant factor.

Conceição, a former Olympic champion who previously campaigned at 130 pounds, showed toughness by lasting the distance but spent much of the fight trying to solve Muratalla’s jab and body attack. The challenger remained competitive in spots, yet he struggled to slow the champion’s pace or force exchanges on his terms.

If Muratalla decides to move to junior welterweight, he would enter one of boxing’s deepest divisions with his unbeaten record intact and a world title already on his resume. His performance against Conceição confirmed he remains one of the sport’s most technically polished young champions, even if he believes his best boxing will come five pounds heavier.

Sports.title: Richardson Hitchins Sees Opening As Devin Haney Needs Opponent
Sports.content:
That left an opening for another welterweight contender, and Hitchins immediately stepped forward.

Hitchins is coming off a 10-round unanimous decision over Ricardo Salas in his first fight at 147 pounds for Zuffa Boxing. He has publicly pursued a fight with Haney for years, but the circumstances are different now because Haney no longer has an opponent lined up.

The biggest question is not whether Haney notices the challenge. It’s whether fans want the matchup. Both fighters are known for their technical styles, leaving many observers uncertain about the bout’s commercial appeal compared with other names Haney has been linked to.

Hitchins recognized an opportunity and acted on it. With Haney searching for his next opponent, the former IBF light welterweight champion has inserted himself into the conversation at a time when the door may finally be open.

Sports.title: Juan Carlos Becerril Stuns Dylan Capetillo With Third Round TKO
Sports.content:
Becerril (3-0, 2 KOs) stayed composed and waited for his opening. Late in the third round, he landed a crushing left hook that caught Capetillo flush and sent him crashing to the canvas. Capetillo beat the count, but his legs were unsteady, and he struggled to convince referee Thomas Taylor that he was ready to continue.

Taylor halted the contest at 2:59 of the third round, awarding Becerril a technical knockout after deciding Capetillo was no longer able to defend himself. The dramatic finish silenced the crowd and instantly changed the direction of the fight.

Capetillo entered the bout as one of Golden Boy’s youngest professional prospects after turning pro earlier this year. The setback serves as an early reminder of the risks young fighters face against opponents with confidence and punching power, even in the opening stages of their careers.

Becerril, meanwhile, leaves Las Vegas with the biggest victory of his career. After recovering from an early knockdown, the unbeaten Mexican prospect showed composure under pressure and seized his opportunity when it arrived, handing Capetillo the first defeat of his professional career.

Ghana News.title: Ministry of Education clarifies basic school language policy, says foreign languages will remain optional
Ghana News.content:
The Ministry of Education has issued a clarification on the Government's proposed language of instruction policy for basic schools, seeking to dispel widespread misconceptions and reassure the public that foreign languages have not been made compulsory under the revised curriculum.

The clarification follows intense public discussion and speculation over proposed changes to the country's education system, with some reports incorrectly suggesting that pupils would be required to study foreign languages such as French, Arabic and Chinese from the early years of schooling.

In a statement, the Ministry stressed that the revised language policy is designed to improve literacy, learning outcomes and cognitive development by ensuring that children begin their education in a language they understand best before gradually transitioning to English.

According to the Ministry, Ghanaian languages will become the principal medium of instruction from Kindergarten (KG) to Primary Three under the proposed revised curriculum.

Education authorities explained that the approach is intended to strengthen children's foundational literacy and numeracy skills while promoting critical thinking and overall cognitive development during their formative years.

The Ministry noted that research conducted across the world consistently demonstrates that children achieve better educational outcomes when they are taught in a familiar language during the early stages of their education.

Learning in a language they already understand enables pupils to grasp concepts more quickly, participate confidently in classroom activities and develop stronger communication skills.

Officials believe the policy will lay a stronger educational foundation for pupils while reinforcing Ghana's rich linguistic and cultural identity.

The revised curriculum proposes a gradual transition beginning in Primary Four, when both Ghanaian languages and English will be used as the medium of instruction until Primary Six.

The Ministry said the bilingual model is intended to ensure pupils are adequately prepared for higher levels of education, where English increasingly becomes the dominant language of instruction.

At the same time, maintaining Ghanaian languages alongside English is expected to preserve learners' proficiency in their mother tongues, encourage multilingualism and prevent the gradual erosion of indigenous languages.

Addressing one of the most debated aspects of the proposed curriculum, the Ministry categorically stated that foreign languages—including French, Arabic and Chinese—will remain optional rather than compulsory subjects.

It explained that these languages will only be offered to pupils who wish to acquire additional language skills and where schools have the necessary teaching staff and learning resources.

The Ministry therefore dismissed claims circulating on social media and other platforms that every pupil would be required to study one or more foreign languages under the revised curriculum.

Officials urged the public to rely on official government communication rather than unverified reports regarding education reforms.

The Ministry said the revised language policy is informed by internationally recognised educational principles, which recommend that children begin learning in their first language before gradually acquiring additional languages.

Research by educational institutions and international organisations has consistently shown that early instruction in a familiar language improves literacy, comprehension, classroom participation and long-term academic performance.

The Ministry said the policy also aligns with Ghana's broader educational objectives of improving literacy standards, promoting multilingual education and preserving the country's diverse linguistic and cultural heritage.

By encouraging competence in both Ghanaian languages and English, the Government aims to produce learners who are academically equipped while remaining connected to their cultural roots.

The Ministry called on parents, teachers, school administrators, media organisations and the general public to disregard misinformation surrounding the proposed curriculum.

It reiterated that reports claiming foreign languages have been made compulsory are false and do not reflect the Government's education policy.

Officials encouraged all stakeholders to seek clarification through official Ministry channels before drawing conclusions about proposed reforms.

Reaffirming its commitment to strengthening Ghana's education system, the Ministry said it remains focused on implementing evidence-based policies that improve teaching and learning across the country.

Ghana News.title: Otumfuo urges KNUST’s new Vice-Chancellor to lead through dialogue, not command
Ghana News.content:
The Chancellor of the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, has urged the university's newly inaugurated Vice-Chancellor, Professor Christian Agyare, to lead through consultation, dialogue and openness rather than command.

Administering the oath of office to Professor Agyare as KNUST's 13th Vice-Chancellor, the Asantehene said the university's new leader must manage differences through established institutional structures while promoting fairness, mutual respect and transparency.

He cautioned that internal disputes should strengthen rather than weaken public confidence in one of Ghana's leading higher education institutions.

"As a former provost, you have been part of management and are therefore very familiar with the concerns of students, staff, alumni and other stakeholders. Now, becoming a Vice-Chancellor, you must rise above these concerns and provide solutions that inspire confidence," Otumfuo said.

He noted that Professor Agyare's tenure as Provost of the College of Health Sciences had given him a deep appreciation of the expectations of students, staff, alumni and other stakeholders.

However, he said assuming the role of Vice-Chancellor required a broader perspective capable of uniting the university community.

"Your responsibility will be to ensure that differences are managed through the university's established structures, through fairness, respect and openness," he stated.

The Asantehene further stressed that dialogue should remain the primary tool for resolving disagreements within the university.

"Internal challenges should strengthen the institution. Dialogue, rather than command, should guide the resolution of differences and not diminish public confidence in this great university. Leadership may change hands, but the mission of the university remains constant," he added.

Professor Agyare, who succeeds Professor Rita Akosua Dickson as Vice-Chancellor, pledged to build on KNUST's achievements by promoting innovation, strengthening partnerships and fostering a culture of shared responsibility.

"This honour belongs to all of us. Together, let us build on our rich legacy, embrace innovation, strengthen partnerships, and work collectively to transform KNUST into an even greater institution," he said.

"The journey ahead is one of shared purpose, and I invite every member of our community to join hands as we move from excellence to eminence."

The investiture ceremony was attended by members of academia, traditional and religious leaders, as well as political figures.

Chief of Staff at the Presidency, Dr Julius Debrah, also challenged the university's leadership to deepen its contribution to national development by driving innovation and entrepreneurship.

He said Ghana's economic recovery must translate into opportunities for young people through knowledge, enterprise and job creation.

"Our economy has shown signs of recovery. We cannot be satisfied with an economy that grows on paper while too many young people remain outside its opportunities," he said.

"Our task is to convert growth into jobs, knowledge into enterprises and national progress into visible improvements in people's lives. This is where KNUST becomes indispensable."

Ghana News.title: Court of Appeal panel changes are routine, not evidence of interference – Samson Lardy Anyenini
Ghana News.content:
Samson Lardy Anyenini

Private legal practitioner and host of JoyNews’ Newsfile, Samson Lardy Anyenini, has dismissed suggestions that changes in the composition of the Court of Appeal panel that handled the appeal involving former MASLOC Chief Executive Officer, Sedina Christine Tamakloe-Attionu, were an indication of judicial interference.

According to him, such changes are a normal administrative practice within the Court of Appeal and should not be interpreted as an attempt to influence the outcome of cases.

Speaking on JoyNews’ The Law on Sunday, August 2, Mr Lardy Anyenini explained that the Court of Appeal sits in panels of three judges and that different panels may handle various stages of the same case depending on the court’s roster and administrative arrangements.

He noted that when Sedina Tamakloe-Attionu’s appeal first came before the Court of Appeal in February 2026, a panel dealt with preliminary and procedural matters. However, when the substantive appeal was ready for hearing and judgment, a different panel had been assigned to the case.

“It is the standard established practice in the Court of Appeal for different panels to sit on a single case across various stages of the court proceedings,” he said.

Mr Lardy Anyenini explained that interlocutory applications, procedural motions and preliminary matters are assigned to available panels based on the court’s judicial roster, a system designed to ensure efficient case management.

He said litigants could appear before one panel when seeking interim reliefs such as a stay of execution, an injunction, or bail pending appeal, and later appear before another panel when the substantive matter is heard.

According to him, the rotation of panels is an administrative mechanism aimed at distributing the workload of the appellate courts and preventing delays in the justice delivery system.

He stressed that the panel that hears the substantive appeal, considers all written submissions and listens to oral arguments is the same panel that reserves the case for judgment and eventually delivers the decision.

Using the Sedina Tamakloe-Attionu case as an example, he explained that earlier proceedings before the Court of Appeal involved procedural issues, including applications for extensions of time and confirmation that both parties had filed the required documents.

“Once the court is satisfied that all filings have been completed, the panel adjourns the matter for judgment and subsequently delivers its decision,” he said.

He added that decisions made by earlier panels on interlocutory applications remain valid and form part of the record available to the final panel hearing the substantive appeal.

Mr Lardy Anyenini maintained that changes in the composition of Court of Appeal panels are guided by administrative procedures and should not be misconstrued as attempts to influence judicial outcomes.

“Judicial assignments follow neutral roster mechanisms, safeguarding judicial independence and systemic transparency,” he said.

He described the explanation as “Law 101” and urged the public to develop a better understanding of judicial administrative processes before attributing ulterior motives to routine changes in panel composition.

Ghana News.title: Prof. Christian Agyare officially assumes office as KNUST’s 13th Vice-Chancellor
Ghana News.content:
Professor Christian Agyare has officially assumed office as the 13th Vice-Chancellor of the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), succeeding Professor Rita Akosua Dickson, the university's first female Vice-Chancellor.

The investiture ceremony, held on Saturday, brought together the Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, Chief of Staff at the Presidency, Dr Julius Debrah, members of academia, traditional and religious leaders, as well as political figures.

Professor Agyare assumes office with more than two decades of experience in academia, research and university administration, having most recently served as Provost of KNUST's College of Health Sciences.

A Professor of Pharmaceutical Microbiology, he is internationally recognised for his research in natural products pharmacology, antimicrobial resistance, wound healing, ethnopharmacology, parasitology and anticancer drug discovery.

He holds Bachelor of Pharmacy and Master of Pharmacy degrees from KNUST and obtained a Doctor rerum naturalium (Dr. rer. nat.) degree from the University of Münster in Germany.

He later undertook postdoctoral and research appointments at Novartis/Seeding Labs in Boston and the University of California, San Francisco, where his work focused on pharmaceutical research and treatments for parasitic diseases.

Professor Agyare has published more than 200 peer-reviewed research papers and has received over 5,000 citations, with an H-index of 36 and an i10-index of 84.

His research has attracted more than US$11 million in competitive grants from international institutions, including the German Research Foundation, the German Academic Exchange Service, the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council, the Mastercard Foundation and the World Bank.

Within KNUST, he has served in several leadership roles, including on the University Executive Committee, Academic Board, Planning and Resources Committee, Budgetary Committee, and the Appointments and Promotions Committee.

Between 2016 and 2020, he headed the university's Quality Assurance and Planning Unit, where he spearheaded reforms aimed at strengthening institutional governance, accountability and operational efficiency.

As Provost of the College of Health Sciences from 2020, Professor Agyare oversaw the introduction of new undergraduate and postgraduate programmes, expanded postgraduate enrolment and supported the development of academic and health-related infrastructure.

His appointment comes with expectations that he will build on KNUST's reputation as one of Africa's leading science and technology universities by strengthening research, innovation and entrepreneurship.

Professor Agyare has outlined a vision centred on expanding research output, accelerating technology-driven transformation, promoting entrepreneurship and enhancing student-centred learning.

He is a Fellow of the Ghana College of Pharmacists and the Pharmaceutical Society of Ghana, a distinguished alumnus of Prempeh College, a practising pharmacist and a member of the Kwadaso Methodist Church.

Professor Agyare is married to Dr (Pharm.) Charlotte Sena Agyare, and they have three children.

Ghana News.title: MASLOC case: Samson Lardy Anyenini explains why Court of Appeal overturned Sedina’s conviction
Ghana News.content:
Legal analyst and host of JoyNews’ Newsfile and The Law, Samson Lardy Anyenini, has explained the reasoning behind the Court of Appeal’s decision to overturn the conviction of former Microfinance and Small Loans Centre (MASLOC) Chief Executive Officer, Sedina Christine Tamakloe-Attionu.

Speaking on the legal issues surrounding the case, Anyenini said the appellate court’s decision was based largely on its finding that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, as required in criminal trials.

He explained that Sedina Tamakloe-Attionu’s appeal challenged both the substance of the High Court judgment and the validity of several charges brought against her.

According to him, the state had argued that although some of the charges may have been defective, those defects were merely technical and should not have resulted in the conviction being overturned.

However, the Court of Appeal took a different view, ruling that the defects were fundamental and affected the fairness of the proceedings.

Court rejects argument that Sedina was a fugitive who could not appeal

Anyenini explained that one of the state’s arguments was that Sedina should not have been allowed to benefit from the appeal process because she had not participated in the original trial.

She was convicted in absentia after leaving Ghana and was later arrested in the United States before extradition proceedings were initiated.

The state argued that she should have returned to Ghana and faced the legal process before seeking to challenge the conviction.

But the Court of Appeal disagreed, holding that an appeal is a constitutional right.

Anyenini said the judges made it clear that a person’s conduct does not automatically take away the right to challenge a judgment through the courts.

Defective charges weakened prosecution’s case

The legal analyst noted that the court found 34 of the 78 charges against Sedina defective because they did not contain sufficient particulars.

He explained that criminal charges must clearly inform an accused person about the specific allegations they are expected to answer.

“The court’s position was that these were not mere technicalities,” Anyenini said, explaining that the lack of details affected Sedina’s ability to properly defend herself.

Those charges were therefore struck out.

Doubts over GH¢500,000 Obaatanpa transaction

On the allegation involving GH¢500,000 paid to Obaatanpa Microfinance, Anyenini said the Court of Appeal found significant gaps in the prosecution’s evidence.

The prosecution relied on a receipt allegedly showing that Sedina received the money, but the court questioned the authenticity of the document because the original was not produced.

The court also noted that no MASLOC official testified to authenticate the receipt.

Anyenini explained that the court found further doubt in correspondence between MASLOC and Obaatanpa, where the institution continued demanding interest on the money.

The judges concluded that those communications suggested uncertainty over whether Sedina had actually taken and retained the funds.

Under criminal law, he noted, such doubt must benefit the accused.

Failure to call key witnesses

Anyenini further explained that the Court of Appeal criticised the prosecution’s reliance on reports and second-hand accounts without calling key witnesses.

On the alleged GH¢1.8 million financial literacy programme, the court noted that the prosecution did not call beneficiaries or regional MASLOC officials who could confirm that the programme did not take place.

Similarly, in the Kantamanto fire relief funds case, the prosecution failed to call the people responsible for distributing the funds or the beneficiaries who were supposed to receive them.

The court therefore found that the allegations were not proven beyond reasonable doubt.

Vehicle procurement and end-of-tenure payments

On the controversial purchase of 350 vehicles, Anyenini said the Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to establish criminal wrongdoing by Sedina.

The court noted that the procurement process had received approvals from relevant institutions and that payments were eventually completed by a later administration.

The judges questioned why the process was allowed to continue if the transaction was considered unlawful.

Regarding end-of-tenure benefits and leave payments, Anyenini said the court relied on testimony from an MASLOC accountant who confirmed that the payments were approved after reviewing the relevant documents.

Burden of proof remained with prosecution

Summarising the judgment, Samson Lardy Anyenini said the central issue was the burden of proof.

He explained that the Court of Appeal found that the trial judge had wrongly placed some responsibility on Sedina to explain or disprove allegations, when the law requires the prosecution to establish guilt.

The appellate court held that Sedina’s absence from the original trial did not remove the state’s obligation to prove every element of the offences.

The Court of Appeal consequently overturned the conviction and acquitted and discharged Sedina Tamakloe-Attionu, bringing an end to a case that had focused national attention on accountability and public financial management at MASLOC.

Ghana News.title: A quiet day in Harare after Zimbabwe’s shutdown call
Ghana News.content:
Harare’s streets have been quieter than usual as residents wait to see whether a call for a nationwide shutdown against constitutional changes would lead to protests.

The first thing that stood out was the traffic.

Cars on the roads leading into the city centre on Friday were fewer than usual. The morning rush hour that normally fills the capital’s streets was missing, and the journey into Harare’s central business district was quicker than expected.

For a normal working day in Zimbabwe, the difference was noticeable.

Police were deployed across Harare as opposition groups and civil society activists called for a nationwide shutdown over constitutional changes. Critics said the amendments could extend President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s time in office until 2030.

Across the city, the security presence was difficult to miss.

Police blocked access to a popular park where people often gather, making it clear that no one would be allowed inside. Nearby, water cannon trucks were parked in an open space that has been used for previous demonstrations.

An uneasy morning

By about 8:30 am (06:30 GMT), parts of Harare’s central business district were slowly coming to life.

In areas where taxis operate and small businesses line the streets, some shops had opened while others remained closed.

The heavy police presence showed that authorities were prepared for possible demonstrations, which police have banned.

In Zimbabwe, public gatherings require police approval, and opposition groups have repeatedly criticised restrictions on protests.

As the day continued, Harare remained calm.

The dispute behind the shutdown

The shutdown call followed constitutional amendments approved by Zimbabwe’s Parliament and signed into law in July.

The changes move the next presidential election from 2028 to 2030 and extend presidential and parliamentary terms from five years to seven.

They also change how future presidents are chosen, replacing a direct presidential election by voters with a system in which the president would be elected by parliament.

Mnangagwa came to power in 2017 after longtime leader Robert Mugabe was removed from office.

He won elections in 2018 and 2023 and was previously expected to leave office at the end of his second term in 2028.

The amendments have drawn criticism from opposition groups and civil society organisations that argue they could allow Mnangagwa to remain in office beyond 2028.

The government has defended the changes, saying they are aimed at reducing political tensions and creating greater stability.

A fight over the liberation legacy

For Godfrey Gurira, who fought in Zimbabwe’s liberation war, the constitutional changes represent a betrayal of the ideals he fought for.

“When we went to war, we were fighting for the people,” he told Al Jazeera.

“We were fighting for one man, one vote. That’s what we want to see happening. We were not fighting for a dynasty or anything along those lines.”

The ruling ZANU-PF party has governed Zimbabwe since independence in 1980. The party has rejected accusations that the amendments are designed to extend Mnangagwa’s time in office.

The government’s defence

Farai Marapira, the ZANU-PF’s information and publicity director, told Al Jazeera that the constitutional changes were intended to address political tensions linked to Zimbabwe’s electoral cycle.

“We have noted that there is a sequence which follows a five-year electoral cycle,” he said.

“Within the first two years, there is contestation of the previous election. In the third year, there is mobilisation for the next election.”

Marapira said the changes would reduce periods of heightened political tension before elections.

Opposition groups disagreed, saying the amendments weaken democratic accountability.

A quiet day, but the dispute continues

The shutdown call did not lead to widespread disruptions in Harare.

As the day continued, the city gradually returned to its normal rhythm.

More shops opened. Taxis returned to the streets. Traffic increased.

But the constitutional amendments that triggered the shutdown call remain contentious.

Opposition groups and activists are challenging the changes in the Constitutional Court while the government continues to defend them.

By the afternoon, Harare had largely returned to its normal weekday routine. But the dispute that brought police onto the streets and prompted the shutdown call is not over.

Ghana News.title: UPSA Law School Roundtable charts path for regulating digital assets in Ghana
Ghana News.content:
The University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA) has led a national conversation on regulating Ghana’s fast-growing digital asset space, with experts calling for a balance between innovation, consumer protection and financial stability.

The 2026 edition of the 14th Absa-UPSA Law School Quarterly Banking Roundtable brought together resource persons with extensive expertise in capital markets and digital asset management.

The forum, which was organized by the UPSA Law School in partnership with Absa Bank Ghana on the theme: “Digital Assets Regulation in Ghana: Navigating Opportunities and Risks.

The Acting Head of the Virtual Assets Department at the Bank of Ghana, Mr. Philip Kwaw Sebuabe, was represented by Mr. Tahiru Alhassan, Head of Oversight and Compliance of the Virtual Assets Department, Bank of Ghana.

Speaking on his behalf, Mr. Alhassan said Ghana’s new Virtual Asset Service Providers Act adopts a risk-based and technology-neutral approach. According to him, the law avoids both an outright ban and a completely unregulated market.

He explained that regulators used a pre-legislative policy sandbox to study emerging business models before finalizing the operational framework. “Consumer protection remains central to the regime,” Mr. Alhassan stated.

He outlined requirements on capital adequacy, custody of client assets, and strict compliance with anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing rules.

Fintech law expert and Co-Founder of Asiedu & Yorke, Kwesi Dadzie-Yorke Esq., described the Act as a major step toward giving the digital asset sector regulatory legitimacy.

He said formal supervision could improve access to banking services, boost investor confidence, and allow licensed firms to prove their regulatory standing. However, he warned that challenges such as fraud, high compliance costs, and counterparty risks remain.

He urged operators to deploy automated sanctions-screening systems and strong contractual safeguards. The panel, which also included Dr. Virág Blazsek, Associate Professor of Law at the University of Leeds, agreed that Ghana’s principles-based framework provides flexibility to respond to new developments such as tokenisation, decentralised finance and stablecoins.

Mr. Alhassan, however, cautioned against foreign currency-backed stablecoins, describing it as “dollarisation on the blockchain.”

He added that cedi-backed stablecoins could be tested within a regulatory sandbox.

In his welcome address, Director of the UPSA Law School, Prof. Kofi Abotsi, said the roundtable forms part of UPSA Law School’s efforts to bridge academic research with regulatory and industry expertise to support Ghana’s digital financial transformation.

Ghana News.title: MASLOC case: How alleged financial irregularities under Sedina triggered investigations and 78 charges
Ghana News.content:
Private legal practitioner, Samson Lardy Anyenini has explained how the criminal case against former Microfinance and Small Loans Centre (MASLOC) Chief Executive Officer, Sedina Christine Tamakloe Attionu, was built around a series of alleged financial irregularities that investigators said occurred during her tenure between 2013 and 2017.

The allegations, which eventually led to a trial involving 78 charges, followed audits and investigations by state agencies, including the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO), into transactions carried out under her leadership.

According to the prosecution’s case, the investigations did not stem from a single transaction but from a pattern of activities across four major areas of MASLOC’s operations: investments in microfinance companies, a financial literacy programme, support for Kantamanto fire victims, and the procurement of vehicles and other items.

Obaatanpa Microfinance transaction

Mr Anyenini said one of the earliest issues that reportedly drew investigators’ attention was a transaction involving Obaatanpa Microfinance in 2014.

MASLOC had initially invested GH¢150,000 in the company before approving an additional GH¢500,000 facility.

The prosecution alleged that after MASLOC issued an Agricultural Development Bank (ADB) cheque for the investment, disagreements arose over the interest rate the company was expected to pay.

He added that the state claimed Sedina Tamakloe demanded a 24 per cent return for MASLOC, but Obaatanpa rejected the arrangement, leading to a request for the return of the funds.

Investigators alleged that when Obaatanpa attempted to refund the money by cheque, the former MASLOC CEO insisted on receiving cash instead.

The prosecution further claimed that the GH¢500,000 was delivered to her in a Ghana Must Go bag at a filling station in Accra.

According to him, investigators considered the refusal of a cheque payment suspicious, arguing that it raised concerns about the handling of public funds.

Financial literacy programme allegations

Another area investigated was a financial literacy programme for MASLOC beneficiaries.

The lawyer noted that MASLOC had secured approval of about GH¢1.7 million for sensitisation programmes targeted at about 85,000 beneficiaries.

The prosecution alleged that only about GH¢1,300 was actually spent on the activity, while the remaining funds were misappropriated.

The state argued that the money meant for educating loan beneficiaries was diverted, resulting in financial loss to the state.

Kantamanto fire relief funds

The investigation also examined funds allocated to support traders affected by a fire disaster at Kantamanto Market, he said.

According to Mr Anyenini, the government had allocated about GH¢1.5 million for the intervention, which was expected to be channelled through a microfinance company for distribution to affected traders.

However, prosecutors alleged that the funds were not used for their intended purpose and that more than GH¢500,000 was lost in the process.

Vehicle procurement controversy

A major component of the case involved the purchase of 350 vehicles for MASLOC.

The prosecution alleged that the vehicles were purchased at inflated prices, creating significant financial losses for the state.

Among the vehicles cited were Chevrolet Isuzu vehicles allegedly purchased at nearly GH¢75,000 each, despite an estimated market value of about GH¢47,000.

The state also questioned the purchase price of 37-seater Isuzu buses, which were allegedly acquired at more than GH¢440,000 each, compared to an estimated market price of about GH¢150,000.

Investigators also raised concerns about the procurement of dual-SIM mobile phones, alleging that MASLOC paid nearly GH¢93,000 for devices that had a market value of about GH¢24,000.

The prosecution estimated that the alleged inflated contracts created a direct loss of more than GH¢22 million.

End-of-tenure payments

The former CEO and her deputy, Wamizana Boubakar, were also accused of receiving unauthorised end-of-tenure benefits after a change in government.

The prosecution alleged that Sedina Tamakloe received more than GH¢270,000 in payments described as unapproved ex-gratia and leave-related benefits.

The state argued that the payments were not properly authorised.

From investigations to prosecution

The allegations, according to prosecutors, amounted to an estimated direct loss of more than GH¢25 million to the state, alongside commitments of over GH¢61 million through what they described as unapproved supply obligations.

These findings formed the basis of the criminal charges filed against Sedina Tamakloe and her operations manager.

However, after years of legal proceedings, the Court of Appeal later acquitted and discharged the former MASLOC CEO, bringing an end to a case that had centred on questions of public financial management, procurement, and accountability.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.
