World.title: A petrol price below R14: What will it take?
World.content:
Will South Africa's petrol price ever get back to below R14? Image: Unsplash

Wouldn’t it be nice to fill your tank cheaply? An entire generation of South Africans learned to drive, got their licences, and bought cars, never knowing the feeling of an under R14 petrol price. That could change under the perfect conditions.

When was the petrol price R14?

2018 was the last time 95 octane fuel was reliably under R14 a litre. March 2018 to be exact. At the time, you could buy petrol inland for R13.76 a litre. This price was higher than the average of the time, when petrol fluctuated between R12 and R13 a litre.

Again, in May 2020, during the COVID-19 lockdowns, the petrol price repeatedly dropped to below R14. But never for periods longer than three months.



What is different now compared to back then, and what would it take for South Africans to experience affordable fuel again?

Brent Crude Needs to Drop Below $50 a Barrel

According to the Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources (DMPR), in January 2017, the average dated Brent Crude price per barrel was $53.45 (R740.81 at the time). In July of that year, it dropped below $50 a barrel, to $46.48 (R598.19 in 2017) before jumping back up to $51.66 (R682.42) in September 2017.

The average dated Brent Crude price would not drop below $50 for another three years.



Then the COVID-19 pandemic brought travelling to a halt.

The price of Brent Crude plummeted. Between April 2020 and January 2021, the average dated Brent crude price fluctuated between $18.99 (R350.74 in May 2020) and $49.20 (R734.55 in January 2021) per barrel.

It hasn’t dropped below $50 a barrel since.

The Rand Must Strengthen Against the Dollar

When the price of petrol was reliably under R14 a litre, the rand traded below R14 to the dollar.



For most of 2017, the rand traded at less than R13.80 to the dollar. The only exception was January 2017 when it was R13.86. Then again in December, it surpassed R14 to the dollar, reaching R14.09.

The same applied to 2019. However, in the final three months of the year, the rand traded at above R14.

Since then, the rand has weakened, with a peak above R19. The currency strengthened slowly from that peak and remains below R17 to the dollar. Yet it has not returned to a rate below R14 since July 2021, when it briefly dipped below R14.



Year Brent Crude Average ($) Rand/Dollar Average 2017 $53.30 R13.37 2018 $71.79 R13.13 2019 $63.42 R16.39 2020 $43.15 R16.40 2021 $68 R14.73 2022 $97.86 R16.25 2023 $82.79 R18.31 2024 $82.77 R18.63** 2026 $82.31 R16.49**

**Only partial data available.

Prices are based on the DMPR’s petrol price archive, which only has records until July 2024 and June 2026.

The Fuel Levy and Road Accident Fund Shouldn’t Increase

According to this table, the price of petrol should be at 2022 levels. However, that wouldn’t be possible since the fuel levy has steadily increased. In March 2017, it was R2.85. Today, it’s R4.29.



The Road Accident Fund (RAF) contribution was R1.63 in 2017; as of 2025, it’s R2.18.

Transport Costs and Retail Margins Must Stabilise

The unfortunate thing about petrol is that when fuel prices rise, transporting petrol becomes more expensive; for inland provinces, this exaggerates an already inflated price.

Retailers also need to get their piece of the pie.



As everything has slowly become more expensive, so too has the retail margin. Surprisingly, the margin has only increased by 80% in 9 years despite petrol increasing by 85%.

Fuel price breakdown in March 2017 compared to August 2026

The DMPR has stressed these are only guidelines. However, they give drivers insight into why petrol costs as much as it does.



Item March 2017 August 2026 Basic Fuel Price R6.12 R14.68 Fuel Levy R2.85 R4.29 Road Accident Fund R1.54 R2.25 Transport Cost R0.41 R0.87 Retail Margin R1.76 R3.15 Total R12.68 R25.24

*Estimates based on October 2025 reporting.

These are some of the conditions South Africans should want, as it will make petrol affordable again.

World.title: ‘My pension is R2400, my rent is R3700’: Pensioner’s SASSA struggle exposed
World.content:
Following The South African’s coverage of SASSA old-age grant amounts, one commenter’s stark breakdown of monthly survival on a pension has struck a nerve with readers, sparking a wider conversation about whether the grant was ever designed to cover the true cost of living in South Africa today.

Sidney Mileham laid out the harsh reality in a single sentence that summed up the frustrations of many pensioners: “Fully agree my pension is R2400 my rent is R3700 excluding lights and water.” The shortfall of over a thousand rand, before a single light bulb or drop of water is even accounted for, immediately drew sympathy and shock in the replies that followed, with many pointing out that the numbers simply don’t work for anyone trying to live independently.

Food costs add another layer of hardship

Fatima Karodia picked up on the gap Mileham described, pointing to a second, equally pressing problem. She asked “and what about food? Prices are so high you look and walk pass some of them,” highlighting how grant recipients are often forced to choose between paying rent and putting meals on the table.



Her comment reflects a pattern seen across SASSA-related discussions, where the grant, once rent and basic bills are factored in, leaves little to nothing for groceries.

Not everyone agrees on what the grant is for

The thread wasn’t without pushback. Ayeza Amathamsanqa challenged the framing of the conversation entirely, arguing that “the money is not for your rent though,” suggesting the grant was never intended to function as a full income replacement.

Others took a more political turn in response to the hardship described. Barney Barnard called for accountability from those in power, saying, “Give ANC 2400 pm and see if they can cope,” while Andre Visser weighed in with a broader economic take, remarking that “a communist society works very well as long as capitalism is healthy and in place.”

Together, the exchange paints a vivid picture of the real arithmetic pensioners are up against, a pension that falls short of rent alone, food prices that add further pressure, and a public divided over what the grant should realistically be expected to cover.
