World.title: FEDCOC Head urges businesses to join new licensing system
World.content:
Chairman of the Federation of Egyptian Chambers of Commerce (FEDCOC) Ahmed al-Wakil described the new public shop licensing system as a “historic opportunity” to integrate informal businesses into the formal economy, urging traders and business owners to take advantage of government incentives to regularize their operations.

al-Wakil praised the government’s efforts to simplify licensing procedures through the Digital Egypt platform, highlighting reduced fees, streamlined services and discounts of up to 50% during the initial implementation phase.

He said the system would improve the business environment by expanding the formal economy, enhancing transparency by publishing all official fees online, and preventing unauthorized charges.

al-Wakil also called for expanding the platform’s services to cover sole proprietorships, partnerships, and small businesses across the Suez Canal and Sinai regions, pledging that local chambers of commerce would provide technical support, awareness campaigns, and digital assistance to help businesses transition to the new system.

World.title: Damietta Port receives 13 vessels in 24 hours
World.content:
“Damietta Port received 13 vessels and recorded the departure of nine ships over the past 24 hours, bringing the total number of vessels at the port to 32,” according to the Damietta Port Authority.

The port handled 15,217 tons of export cargo, including beet pulp feed, gypsum, bagged cement, urea and other goods. Imports reached 20,515 tons, consisting of scrap metal, beech wood, steel, rice and plywood.

Container traffic included 550 export containers, 242 import containers and 3,912 transit containers.

The port’s public grain silos contained 84,641 tons of wheat, while private storage facilities held 44,430 tons. Truck traffic totaled 2,798 movements during the reporting period.

Meanwhile, the GALLIPOLI SEAWAYS Ro-Ro vessel departed for Trieste, Italy, carrying 3,704 tons of cargo, including agricultural products, textiles, garments, electrical cables, automotive parts, buses, machinery and industrial equipment.

The cargo was bound for several European destinations, including Italy, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, France, Austria, Sweden, Poland, Slovenia, Slovakia and Hungary, while transit shipments were destined for the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Bahrain.

World.title: Abdelatty congratulates Yemen’s new FM, reaffirms Egypt’s backing
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty has congratulated Yemen’s newly appointed Foreign Minister Afrah Abdulaziz Al-Zouba during a phone call on Saturday, August 1, 2026.

Abdelatty reaffirmed Egypt’s commitment to strengthening bilateral ties and supporting Yemen’s stability, lauding longstanding fraternal relations between the two countries and underscoring Cairo’s keenness to deepen cooperation and coordination across various fields.

The talks focused on the latest developments in Yemen, as Abdelatty reiterated Egypt’s unwavering support for the Arab country’s unity, territorial integrity and legitimate government, in line with relevant international resolutions.

He stressed the importance of supporting Yemen’s national institutions to help restore security and stability and meet the aspirations of the Yemeni people.

The two ministers also exchanged views on regional developments and emphasized the need to continue efforts toward a comprehensive political settlement that preserves Yemen’s unity and contributes to broader regional stability.

World.title: Chief Mumena Ordered To Pay K600,000 To Torture Victims
World.content:
The Lusaka High Court has ordered Chief Mumena and the Attorney General to jointly pay more than K600,000 to three members of one family after finding the traditional leader unlawfully detained, tortured and forced them into labour over accusations that they held court documents challenging his authority.

Judge Geoffrey Mulenga ruled that Chief Mumena, whose real name is Jonathan Eshron Mumena, must personally pay K5,000 to each petitioner and publish a public apology in a newspaper of nationwide circulation within 30 days.

The ordeal began in January 2024, when Loveness Mwanza, Lawrence Kamasanyi and Salon Kalusa, all of Kananga area in North-Western Province, were forcibly taken from their homes on the chief’s orders. They were held in a metal container without basic sanitation or ventilation, assaulted, forced to perform labour and denied adequate food, water and medical care.

For Kalusa, who depends on antiretroviral medication, the consequences proved especially severe. He was cut off from his treatment during the detention, causing his health to deteriorate seriously. The family later filed a petition against the chief and the Attorney General in November 2024, arguing that their constitutional rights had been violated and that the State had failed in its duty to intervene once it became aware of the abuse.

Chief Mumena never appeared in court to answer the allegations. In his judgment, Mulenga noted that although duly served with court process, the chief neither entered an appearance nor led evidence in rebuttal, leaving the petitioners’ account of events entirely unchallenged.

The court found that the petitioners’ rights under Articles 11, 13, 14, 15, 17 and 22 of the Constitution had been violated. Mulenga further held the Attorney General jointly and severally liable, ruling that the State had failed to prevent or stop the abuses despite being aware of the petitioners’ unlawful confinement and mistreatment.

The judge described Chief Mumena’s conduct as displaying “contumelious disregard” for both the petitioners’ constitutional rights and the authority of the court, noting that he had ignored court summons and shown no remorse throughout the proceedings.

Mwanza was awarded K175,000 in damages for unlawful detention, battery, torture, forced labour and inhuman treatment, plus K30,000 in exemplary damages, bringing her total award to K205,000.

Kamasanyi, who suffered permanent injuries including swelling and tenderness to his right scrotum, was awarded K185,000 in compensatory damages and K30,000 in exemplary damages, for a total of K210,000.

Kalusa was awarded K185,000 in compensatory damages and K35,000 in exemplary damages for the deterioration in his health, giving him a total of K220,000.

Beyond the compensation, Chief Mumena must personally pay K5,000 to each petitioner, while the petitioners were also awarded legal costs to be agreed or taxed.

World.title: EIZ optimistic on new fees regulation
World.content:
EIZ is optimistic new fees regulation will align engineering sector and protect consumers

By David Kamungu

Like lawyers, accountants and other professionals that have gazetted guidelines on fees that they are required to charge for their services, the government has approved new regulation regulating pricing engineering professional services in Zambia.

Until now, the engineering sector in Zambia has existed without a framework that regulates the minimum chargeable fees by engineers due to lack of enabling legislation to ensure total professionalism in pricing by eliminating unhealthy competition such as undercutting in pricing during bidding processes.

The unregulated pricing of engineering services has had many pitfalls.

In some cases, some providers of engineering services, in desperate bids to win certain tenders, have resorted to undercutting rivals with dire consequences on both the engineering service providers and the consumers as the quality of the final product tends to be below prescribed and acceptable standards.

And this is why the recently government approved Engineering Institution of Zambia (Professional Service Fees) Regulations, 2026 also referred to as S.I No. 34 of 2026 is being held as a “significant milestone” for the local engineering sector.

So, S.I No. 34 of 2026 is essentially aimed at streamlining and aligning the engineering sector and professional practice by providing guidelines for professional fees to be charged for services rendered by engineering professionals.

“The whole purpose is not merely to prescribe fees but to promote professionalism and generally, the quality service of work. And therefore, by providing this transparency fees structure, our members are better positioned to dictate the necessary expertise, time and resources required to deliver engineering services,” Engineering Institution of Zambia (EIZ) Chief Executive Officer and Registrar Eng. David Kamungu said in an interview.

“In terms of what these fees mean to EIZ members like other regulated professions such as law, architecture here in Zambia, engineering now has an approved framework that recognizes the value of the professional services.”

Eng. Kamungu emphasized that the prescribed fees to apply to professional engineering services rendered by qualified practitioners should not be misinterpreted as employment remuneration.

According to Zambian labour laws which are also consistent with international best practices, employment remuneration is compensated through a salary – a fixed amount paid by an employer to an employee as compensation for ongoing employment, usually on a monthly basis and determined by employment contracts, organisational salary structures, and collective agreements among other considerations.

On the other hand professional service fee is the amount charged for specialised professional services provided by an independent, qualified and licensed practitioner or professional firm for a specific assignment, project or consultancy.

These fees are charged only when professional services are engaged and are intended to compensate the professional for the expertise, responsibility, time, skill and experience required to perform the work.

For a long time in Zambia, the engineering profession has not been able to regulate the minimum chargeable by engineers due to a lack of enabling legislation.

This absence of legislation to regulate the minimum chargeable fees by engineers has exposed consumers of engineering services to unhealthy competition such as undercutting as there has been no adequate buffer against harmful practices.

“For our members, this provides clarity and they also provide consistency and fairness in the pricing of engineering services. They also help eliminate unfair price competition but also protect the integrity of the profession in ensuring that only experts are approved to perform these jobs,” Eng. Kamungu said.

In the build-up to the formulation of S.I No. 34 of 2026 Regulations, some stakeholders expressed reservation that the standardizing of minimum Professional Service Fees could lead to an increase in cost of accessing engineering services in the country.

But with any functioning legislation, the formulation of new law regulating the minimum Professional Service Fees for engineering services was done with a specific focus on consumer protection which is at the core of any rational and ethical business practice.

The focus of S.I No. 34 of 2026 is to ensure consumer protection is implemented and enforced through minimum fees that are considered fair, consistent with required quality and meet minimum professional standards.

“Regarding the concerns, it is important to appreciate that quality Engineering is an investment rather than a cost. The objective of these regulations is not to make Engineering services expensive, but to ensure the delivery of professionally and sustainably but also equally by the service providers,” Eng. Kamungu explained. `

Who Is Eligible to charge Professional Fees?

The approved professional services fees only apply to members that hold valid EIZ practicing certificates such registered Professional Engineers, Engineering Technologists, Engineering technicians and registered engineering Craftspersons among others.

“So, those are members that have our registration certificates that are issued in accordance with the Engineering Registration Board,” says Eng. Kamungu.

How are the Professional fees going to be charged?

Typical of any assignment where professional services are billed according to the time spent on the work, the Regulations prescribe hourly fee rates expressed in fee units varied through the practitioner’s professional classification, years of relevant experience and the category of engineering professional among other considerations.

To determine the actual monetary amount chargeable per hour, the prescribed fee units are multiplied by the current Fee Unit Value established under Statutory Instrument No. 25 of 2024, which is presently K0.40 (40 Ngwee) per fee unit.

World.title: Cancer Diseases Hospital reopens after US$31 million upgrade
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has commissioned the refurbished radiotherapy and imaging section at Cancer Diseases Hospital in Lusaka, restoring specialised cancer treatment services that had been suspended for six years.

The US$31 million facility, fully funded by the Zambian Government, makes Zambia one of only three African countries with advanced dedicated cancer care capacity, alongside South Africa and Egypt.

Hichilema described the commissioning as a prayer answered for hundreds of cancer patients across the country. “All of you cancer patients out there, your prayers have been answered. I am talking about over 800 cancer patients who have been waiting in the queue to go for treatment in India and other countries,” he said.

The radiotherapy and imaging services were suspended in 2020 to allow for the transformation of the hospital into what the President described as a world-class cancer treatment centre. The reopening was achieved without external funding.

The first patient to receive treatment at the upgraded facility was Maureya Zimba, 62, a cervical cancer patient whose testimony visibly moved the President.

“How satisfying it is to hear Madam Maureya Zimba, a 62-year-old cervical cancer patient, being the first patient to undergo treatment here. Her treatment was more than a medical procedure; it is a mark of hope for many cancer patients among the 21 million Zambians,” Hichilema said.

Zimba expressed gratitude to the President and urged him to continue the development agenda his administration has pursued.

Hichilema announced that the Ndola Cancer Treatment Centre, now 85 percent complete, will be commissioned before the end of the year. He also directed Ministry of Health permanent secretary for technical services Kennedy Lishimpi to expedite construction of the Livingstone Cancer Centre, which will serve the southern and western parts of the country.

The President further revealed plans are under way to build a medical city near Kenneth Kaunda International Airport to promote health tourism.

He disclosed that his administration had cleared a legacy debt owed to Indian hospitals for the treatment of Zambian cancer patients, debt that had accumulated under the previous government.

“We had to clear it because Indian hospitals started refusing to treat cancer patients, so we cleared it and said bye, bye,” he said.

Hichilema cautioned health workers against spending excessive time on their mobile phones while on duty, saying the facility’s network access would be restricted except for digital consultation purposes.

“I do not expect phones here. The system should ensure that everyone who works here does not come in with a phone. We will even obliterate the network here unless you want to deal with digital consultations,” he said.

Secretary to Cabinet Patrick Kangwa, speaking through remarks read on his behalf by Presidential Delivery Unit head Kusobile Kamwambi, said the President’s priority directive was to ensure quality healthcare, resulting in an 80 percent availability of medicines in health facilities across the country.

Kangwa said the expansion of digital hospitals, recruitment of health workers and construction of maternity annexes stand as evidence of the President’s commitment to improving healthcare.

German Ambassador to Zambia Sonke Siemon welcomed the selection of a German company to undertake the refurbishment of the centre, saying Germany remains committed to partnering with Zambia to strengthen the country’s healthcare system.

Lishimpi said in his opening remarks that the hospital had accumulated a backlog of 1,600 patients following the suspension of radiotherapy services in 2020.

Siemens Healthineers Southern Africa chief executive officer Ayanda Swana said the newly installed equipment has the capacity to treat up to 3,000 patients annually.

Cancer Diseases Hospital senior medical superintendent Dr Susan Msadabwe said the reopening of the radiotherapy unit would significantly improve access to treatment, allowing more patients to receive specialised cancer care within the country.

The hospital has also installed a new CT simulator to enhance the precision of radiotherapy planning, with a second CT simulator already being installed to expand capacity further. Chief radiation therapist Dr Ncheebe Sidaza said the simulator serves as the initial stage of treatment planning, allowing clinicians to map tumours accurately before patients begin therapy on the hospital’s linear accelerators

World.title: Mundubile launches public campaign funding appeal
World.content:
Opposition presidential candidate Brian Mundubile has launched a public fundraising drive for his campaign, inviting ordinary Zambians to bankroll his bid for the presidency with the national vote fast approaching.

The National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity leader announced the initiative in a Facebook post on Saturday, describing it as a “people-driven campaign” and urging citizens to make voluntary contributions towards party activities.

The move places Mundubile’s financing strategy in the same category as that once associated with constitutional lawyer John Sangwa, who built his Movement for National Renewal candidacy around the same citizen-funded model before withdrawing from the race earlier this year, citing registration delays and fears among supporters over the traceability of contributions.

Mundubile disclosed no fundraising target and gave no indication of how contributions would be collected or accounted for. The post directed supporters to a newly launched campaign support platform.

The NRPUP candidate paired the appeal with a policy pledge, promising to revise school grants upwards once he forms government. He offered no detail on the scale of the proposed increase or its funding source.

UPND supporters have moved swiftly to criticise the fundraising appeal on social media, framing it as evidence of a struggling campaign. The mockery, however, sits awkwardly against President Hakainde Hichilema’s own fundraising history. In September 2015, ahead of the 2016 election, Hichilema publicly promoted a donation platform, HH-Zambia.com, urging supporters to “spread the word” that his campaign could now receive donations. He renewed the approach in 2021, running a GoFundMe page titled “Hakainde Hichilema-2021 Presidential Fundraiser,” which accepted small individual donations processed through the platform.

Both fundraising drives were run openly and publicly, mirroring the model Mundubile has now adopted.

The announcement lands at a sensitive point in the campaign calendar. With voters set to head to the polls within days, presidential candidates typically shift from broad policy messaging to logistics-heavy final pushes covering transport, rally costs and get-out-the-vote operations, all of which require sustained cash flow.

The NRPUP has campaigned on a platform of national reconciliation and unity, with Mundubile and running mate Makebi Zulu positioning themselves as the primary challenge to Hichilema.

The party has in recent days gained momentum from defections, including former Ngambela Clement Sinyinda, who publicly endorsed the Mundubile-Zulu ticket after withdrawing his support for Hichilema.

Presidential campaigns in Zambia require substantial resources for provincial travel, rally logistics, campaign materials and volunteer coordination, particularly given the country’s geographic spread and infrastructure challenges.

Crowdfunding as a campaign financing model carries both advantages and risks. Supporters argue it strengthens grassroots ownership and reduces dependence on a small number of wealthy backers who might expect political favours in return. Sangwa’s own experience with the model illustrates the risks, as his campaign ultimately stalled partly over difficulties raising funds through the same approach.

Whether Mundubile’s version can generate sufficient resources to compete with better-resourced rivals in the campaign’s closing days remains an open question, particularly in a race already shaping up to be tightly contested.

The NRPUP has not indicated whether it will publish regular updates on funds raised, or whether the platform will remain open through to polling day.

World.title: Copper Queens’ quarterfinal hopes dented after loss to Nigeria
World.content:
The Copper Queens have complicated their chances of advancing to the quarterfinals of the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) after suffering a 1-0 defeat to defending champions Nigeria on Saturday night.

A win for Zambia at Al Madina Stadium would have seen them progress to the last eight with a game to spare.

Instead, Asisat Oshoala’s early strike condemned Bruce Mwape’s former side to their first loss of the tournament.

Oshoala scored in the 8th minute to give the Super Falcons the lead.

Nigeria, who had lost their opener to debutants Malawi, held on until the final whistle to revive their own qualification hopes.

It was a disappointing display for Zambia, who had kicked off the tournament with a dominant 6-0 win over Egypt last Tuesday.

The result has seen the Copper Queens drop from top of Group C to third, remaining on three points.

In the other Group C match played earlier on Saturday, Malawi secured a 3-1 victory over Egypt to book their place in the quarterfinals.

Zambia now face a must-win final group game against Malawi next Wednesday at Al Madina Stadium in Rabat to keep their knockout stage ambitions alive.

The top four semi-finalists at WAFCON will earn automatic qualification to the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

The Copper Queens are aiming to better their bronze medal finish at the 2022 WAFCON, won under the late coach Bruce Mwape.

World.title: Inclusive electoral process, flourishes democracy-ECZ
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) says it recognises that an inclusive electoral process is the cornerstone of a thriving democracy.

Speaking during the ECZ Women’s Conference held at Ndola Skills Training Centre in Ndola today, Copperbelt Provincial Electoral Officer, Shaft Musaka, said women are not just participants in elections, but decision-makers, advocates and architects of a brighter future.

Mr Musaka said the Commission has deliberately implemented policies aimed at empowering women at every stage of the electoral process.

“We have strengthened voter education programmes specifically tailored to address barriers that hinder women’s full participation in elections,” he said.

Mr Musaka said the Commission is also actively promoting women’s representation in electoral administration to ensure their voices are heard, valued and integrated into decision-making structures.

He added that the ECZ continues to champion safe, peaceful and fair elections that are free from intimidation and discrimination, enabling women to vote and contest leadership positions with confidence.

Mr Musaka explained that empowering women requires collective action and collaboration, adding that the Commission is working with communities, organisations and other stakeholders to amplify women’s voices, promote civic engagement, and encourage more women to stand as candidates, election observers and advocates for peaceful and credible elections.

“As we embrace this commitment, let us remind ourselves that peace is not just the absence of conflict; it is the presence of justice, equity and opportunity,” he said.

Mr Musaka urged women in Ndola and across the country to actively participate in shaping Zambia’s democratic future.

“Let this Women’s Conference be a call to action for every woman in Ndola and beyond to rise, participate and shape the future of Zambia’s democracy,” he said.

World.title: Hichilema completes ten-province tour amid Kaingu row
World.content:
Hichilema completes ten-province tour with Western Province pledges as independent candidate Kaingu accuses him of overreach

President Hakainde Hichilema has concluded a nationwide community outreach campaign by pledging a sweep of infrastructure and economic projects for Western Province, becoming the first presidential candidate in the 2026 general election to campaign in all ten provinces. But the closing leg of his tour has also drawn sharp criticism after he urged voters in Mwandi not to support independent parliamentary candidate Iris Kaingu, prompting accusations that he overstepped his role as head of state.

Speaking during engagements in Shang’ombo, Nalolo, Limulunga and Senanga, President Hichilema said his government’s focus for Western Province would be on infrastructure and economic projects that create jobs, improve livelihoods and strengthen cross-border trade with Angola. He told supporters in Shang’ombo that the district’s strategic location and natural resources gave it the potential to become one of Zambia’s most prosperous border towns.

“I see the potential of developing Shang’ombo into a very successful town. We are going to improve the border post so that people trade well with Angola and some of you will be employed there,” he said.

He announced plans to establish an abattoir in the district to allow livestock farmers to process beef locally for export, expand agricultural production to boost food security, improve telecommunications through additional mobile towers, modernise the Shang’ombo airstrip, construct a new market with reliable water supply, establish more boarding secondary schools and build a skills training centre for young people. He also pledged to rehabilitate the Shang’ombo-Rivungo canal through construction of a harbour and related facilities.

The President said the creation of a second constituency in Shang’ombo had already increased Constituency Development Fund allocations from K40 million to K80 million, allowing for faster investment in schools, health facilities, feeder roads and water projects. He said upgrading the Sioma-Shang’ombo road remained a priority.

In Nalolo, he said economic growth would be driven by expanded agricultural productivity, timely Farmer Input Support Programme payments through mobile money platforms, and improved road networks. He pledged to improve mobile network coverage, construct a district hospital, complete government offices and staff houses, and recruit more teachers and health workers.

In Limulunga, President Hichilema said Western Province had enormous untapped potential and announced plans to establish a milk-processing plant, expand fisheries into a commercial enterprise, complete Lewanika University, upgrade Mongu Airport into an international facility, and advance plans for the proposed Sioma Hydro-power Station.

“The upgrading of the Mongu airport is starting soon and we will continue to develop for our people. Running a country is not a joke, one must have the love for the people,” he said.

UPND Liuwa parliamentary candidate and former Finance and National Planning Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane said President Hichilema had demonstrated commitment to Western Province through continued investment in infrastructure and social programmes, and urged residents to support UPND to ensure development programmes continue.

In Senanga, the President apologised for arriving late due to a demanding schedule and appealed to voters to support UPND, saying this would ensure continuity of programmes including free education. He said upgrading the Senanga-Maata road remained a key priority.

The engagements marked the conclusion of the President’s nationwide community outreach programme, which he began earlier in the campaign season and which took him to all ten provinces ahead of the 13 August vote.

However, the tour’s final stretch has been overshadowed by controversy following remarks President Hichilema made in Mwandi on Thursday, where he urged residents not to vote for Iris Kaingu, an aspiring independent parliamentary candidate, because she defied his advice not to contest outside the UPND.

Kaingu, reacting to the remarks, said Zambians have the right to choose the person they want to vote for and should not be forced to support a candidate they do not want. She said she was shocked that the Head of State would attack her in such a manner when she was merely exercising her democratic right to contest as an independent.

“I cannot believe the president came all the way to de-campaign me even when the people of Mwandi have clearly indicated that they do not want the UPND candidate,” she said.

Kaingu also pushed back on the suggestion that Western Province remains loyal UPND territory, arguing that the party’s traditional support base in the province has been eroded by continued underdevelopment.

“If Western Province is UPND’s bedroom, then it is a dirty bedroom, because the people in the province are now suffering, as infrastructure is in a deplorable state,” she said.

Movement for Multi-Party Democracy national secretary Lumba Kalumba condemned the President’s remarks as an affront to democracy, saying that calling an adult woman a “difficult child” and labelling her difficult for refusing to obey was not mere rhetoric but language of subordination.

“It frames her as disrespectful for making independent choices. It reinforces the idea that women in politics must be compliant, not assertive; obedient, not ambitious. A democratic President does not dictate who may or may not stand. He does not use state and party platforms to bully opponents, especially women. He competes on issues, not on intimidation,” Kalumba said in a statement.

She said labelling a woman a “difficult child” set a dangerous precedent for Zambian democracy. “This is not strong leadership. It is an infringement on women’s rights, democratic rights, and the basic principles of a free and fair election,” Kalumba said.

The controversy has also drawn editorial criticism. An opinion piece published this week argued that the remarks in Mwandi sit uneasily alongside the President’s repeated declarations of commitment to increasing women’s participation in leadership, noting that the Constitution expressly recognises independent candidates as a legitimate category of contestant, not a violation of party loyalty.

President Hichilema‘s tour of Western Province, and the broader ten-province outreach it capped, has been framed by his campaign as evidence of a leader personally engaged with every corner of the country ahead of polling day. But the Mwandi remarks have instead become the dominant talking point in the campaign’s closing fortnight, with critics arguing that a sitting president using his platform to campaign against an independent candidate raises questions about the boundaries between incumbency and electoral fairness that voters will now weigh alongside the infrastructure pledges themselves

World.title: Two funerals, two flashpoints: politics intrudes on mourning
World.content:
“No life is worth losing for power,” Chief Chisunka warns as funerals become flashpoints and party accuses police of standing by

Traditional leaders, a Catholic priest and an opposition party chairman have issued pointed warnings against rising political violence ahead of the 13 August general election.

Their intervention comes after two funerals in Eastern and Southern provinces this week descended into standoffs over party politics.

Chief Chisunka of the Ushi people of Luapula said no life is worth losing for the sake of power. He called on politicians to rein in their cadres before the country is set alight.

“We don’t have to lose lives just for certain people to cling to power. Peace needs to prevail because the country has been a beacon of hope,” the chief told The Mast.

He said it was unfortunate that parts of the nation were experiencing bloodshed in what he described as a Christian country. Politicians, he said, needed to sober up and tame their cadres before Zambia is drawn into wider conflict.

The Ushi traditional leader called on chiefs countrywide to rise to the occasion and denounce political violence wherever it occurs.

Catholic priest Father Gladson Phiri echoed the call. He said the church and traditional leaders are best placed to lead the fight against political violence because they deal directly with the citizens who go on to engage in political activity.

“The church and traditional leaders are the ones that should champion the fight against political violence because they usually deal with the masses who in turn engage in various political activities,” Fr Phiri said.

He said clergy and chiefs needed to engage both politicians and the electorate on the dangers of violence, warning that the country risked being set ablaze if the trend continues unchecked.

The warnings came in the same week that two funerals turned into flashpoints, illustrating how deeply campaign season has begun to intrude on ordinary community life.

In Aslot Township, Chipata District, mourners stormed out of Mgwelo Maplot Cemetery on Wednesday. The walkout came the moment a UPND official was called upon to address the gathering.

Both the ruling party and the opposition National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity had contributed toward funeral arrangements for the deceased. UPND gave K400; NRPUP reportedly covered other costs, including transport.

The solemn atmosphere shattered when director of ceremony Goldwin Soko announced that the UPND representative would give remarks. Without warning, a section of mourners rose and left the graveyard in a show of disapproval.

“When funerals are politicised and become battlegrounds, then we have a problem,” Alakwisa Jere, a Chipata-based mourner who witnessed the scene, told The Mast.

The Chipata walkout came barely a day after a similar episode in Mazabuka.

There, District Commissioner Oliver Mulomba was booed by angry residents on Tuesday and forced to abandon his speech. The crowd accused him of campaigning for President Hakainde Hichilema and the UPND at a funeral.

Mr Mulomba had to leave the scene to avoid possible harm.

Jere warned that the Chipata and Mazabuka incidents were a sign of what could unfold as campaigning intensifies in the final stretch before polling day. Leaders from both UPND and opposition parties have since appealed for calm, urging cadres and officials to keep politics out of funerals and other community gatherings.

Separately, Leadership Movement national chairperson David Kalumba accused the Zambia Police Service of failing to act against known perpetrators of political violence.

“Police officers have become spectators of violence,” he said in a statement.

He said his party had campaigned throughout the country encouraging people to reject violence and demand accountability, but that police had “betrayed people it is supposed to protect by failing to stop violence.”

Kalumba said no one should celebrate the destruction of public and private property currently taking place in parts of the country at the hands of political cadres. Zambians, he warned, must reject political violence at all costs, because the aftermath would be difficult to rebuild from.

He stressed that his own party was not a violent movement but a pro-poor organisation focused on building a Zambia with equal job and business opportunities for all.

“Our people have told us that all they want is peace, unity and development, and that is the message we are preaching,” he said.

The Leadership Movement chairman said his party had learnt a great deal on the 2026 campaign trail. Poverty, underdevelopment and lack of opportunity, he said, remain a disease afflicting many communities, particularly in rural areas he accused previous leadership of excluding from the national development agenda.

“Our people in rural areas need development but they cannot see it because previous leadership have excluded them from national development agenda,” Kalumba said.

He pledged that, if voted into office, his party would open access to rural development, working toward better roads, schools, markets, hospitals and clinics for rural communities.

Kalumba said the rural population should remain the main focus for the next five years, noting that the rural vote is larger than the urban vote on the current voter register.

Taken together, the warnings from traditional and religious leaders and the accusations levelled by the Leadership Movement chairman paint a picture of mounting anxiety over the tone of the campaign’s final fortnight. Community leaders are now openly worried that political competition could spill into the kind of bloodshed Zambia has largely avoided in recent electoral cycles.
